title: Civil suit may proceed years after man fatally shot by VicPD officer, judge rules
subtitle: A B.C. Supreme Court judge has ruled that a mom's civil lawsuit against the City of Victoria and VicPD officers for the shooting death of her son may proceed.
article: A B.C. Supreme Court judge has ruled that a mom's civil lawsuit against the City of Victoria and VicPD officers for the shooting death of her son may proceed.
Marney Mutch's son, Rhett Mutch, was fatally shot in the neck by Victoria Police officers on Nov. 1, 2014 after he went to his mother's house despite a "no contact order."

The Independent Investigations Office of B.C. report issued in 2016 said his mother called 911 at 10:51 a.m. and officers arrived at 10:54 a.m. The dispatch said the mom was confronting her son and said he had picked up a knife. IIO says the mother told dispatch and officers "you don't need a gun" and that he was holding the knife to himself repeatedly.
Within three minutes, officers had "made contact" with the son, then at 11:02 a.m. one of the officers reported that shots had been fired.
The IIO report found there was no evidence that the officers had motivation to harm Rhett, and a coroner's inquest ruled his a death a suicide.
Marney had filed a civil lawsuit in November 2016 against the city and seven unnamed VicPD officers, but there have been delays in the case.

In October 2023, the City of Victoria applied to the court to dismiss the case due to "want of prosecution," which means there has been an "inordinate and unexplained delay in advancing a claim (usually longer than about three or four years)," according to Lawson Lundell LLP.

In order for a case to be dismissed due to want of prosecution, a judge must find that there was an inordinate delay, the delay was inexcusable, and that it is not in the interests of justice to continue.

In Marney's case, the B.C. Supreme Court judge found the delay was inordinate, as Marney had taken no steps since November 2016 to advance the case, and the delay was inexcusable, as she had "subjective reasons" for the delay but the judge found them inexcusable. However, it was in the interest of justice to proceed with the case.

The associate judge Sandra Harper found it was in the interest of justice to proceed due, in part, to the fact that Marney is representing herself and "has been disadvantaged by having to prosecute a challenging case as a self-represented litigant."

While the case may proceed, Marney is required to remove some of the aspects of her case in the proceeding lawsuit, including her claims that officers committed purjury, claims about criminal negligence as she did not provide facts to support this claim, and her allegation that Rhett was not informed of the reasons for his detention.
"There are no material facts that allege that Rhett was being detained," the judge wrote in her ruling. "I do not understand this pleading. The pleading is confusing and must be removed."
Marney also filed a request to change the names of the VicPD officers in the civil claim from John Doe 1-7 to include their names, as she learned them since filing the initial suit.
"I conclude that the police officers may be individually named," Harper wrote in the decision.

"Ms. Mutch runs the risk, as does any plaintiff, that if she fails to amend the Proposed Pleading to properly plead the facts and law regarding gross negligence, she may be faced with an application brought by any, or all, of the now-named police officers to strike her pleading."
Marney now has 45 days to file a further amended notice of civil claim that complies with the rules, and 60 days to deliver her list of documents to proceed with the claim.
